nameStory: The name 'winecup' comes from the deep wine-red to purple color of the cup-shaped flowers that look like they could hold a sip of red wine. It's also called 'purple poppy-mallow' because the silky, papery petals resemble those of poppies, though it's actually in the mallow family, not the poppy family.
description: Winecup mallow is a low-growing perennial wildflower with trailing stems that spread along the ground. It produces gorgeous cup-shaped flowers in deep wine-red to magenta colors that are about 2 inches across. The plant has deeply divided, finger-like leaves and forms spreading mats. This Great Plains native is quite rare in New England, where it's found only as an occasional garden escape or naturalized plant.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Deep wine-red to magenta cup-shaped flowers about 2 inches across with five silky, papery petals that feel delicate to the touch and have a slight sheen

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Deeply divided leaves split into 5-7 narrow, finger-like segments that feel slightly fuzzy and rough, arranged alternately along the stems

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Low, spreading plant with trailing stems that hug the ground and can extend 2-3 feet, forming loose mats rather than upright clumps

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Round, flat seed pods that split into wedge-shaped sections, each containing one seed with a slightly wrinkled, hard surface

habitat: In New England, winecup mallow is extremely rare and typically found only in disturbed areas, roadsides, or as garden escapes that have naturalized in sunny, well-drained locations. It prefers sandy or rocky soils and full sun exposure. Since it's native to the Great Plains, it's not naturally part of New England's ecosystem.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges from the root crown as small rosettes of deeply divided leaves, with stems beginning to spread outward along the ground.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming period with wine-colored cup flowers opening in succession from early to late summer, most vibrant in the morning hours.
seasonality.fall: Flowers continue into early fall, followed by the development of distinctive round, flat seed pods that split open when ripe.
seasonality.winter: Above-ground portions die back completely, leaving only a small rosette of leaves close to the ground or just the root crown visible.

funFact: Despite being called 'poppy-mallow,' this plant is actually more closely related to hibiscus and cotton than to poppies, and its flowers can close up on cloudy days or in the afternoon, like they're taking a nap!
confusionNotes: The deep wine-red cup-shaped flowers are quite distinctive and unlikely to be confused with other New England wildflowers. The closest might be wild geraniums, but those have much paler pink-purple flowers and completely different leaf shapes.
contextualKnowledge: The common name 'buffalo rose' hints at its Great Plains heritage, where it grows alongside prairie grasses in buffalo country. Don't let the 'poppy' in 'poppy-mallow' fool you - it's named for the flower's appearance, not its family relationships.
compareHints: Winecup mallow is the only species in its genus found in New England, making it unique in the region. Compared to other mallows like common mallow or marsh mallow, winecup has much more intensely colored flowers and deeply divided leaves rather than rounded or heart-shaped ones. Its trailing growth habit also sets it apart from the more upright growth of most other mallow family members.
